opus-5.5.text:
I think the next big shift is moving from coding as completion to coding as agency. For a while, the question was whether a model could write a correct function, pass a benchmark, or fill in the next few lines. That's largely solved for many everyday cases. The harder and more interesting problem now is whether a model can take a vague goal, explore a real codebase, form a plan, run things, see what breaks, and iterate, the way a good engineer does over hours or days rather than seconds.

That changes what we need to train for. First, long-horizon reasoning: the model has to keep a coherent intention across many steps and not lose track halfway through. Second, environment interaction: reading files, executing tests, using terminals and tools, and treating the feedback from the environment as real signal. That's where reinforcement learning becomes really important, because code gives you something rare in AI, which is verifiable reward. Tests pass or they don't, the program runs or it crashes. That makes coding one of the best playgrounds for scaling RL.

Third, and people underestimate this, is judgment. Knowing when to stop, when to ask the human a clarifying question, when a fix is a hack versus a proper solution. A lot of current agents will happily make the tests green by doing something ugly. Teaching taste and reliability is much harder than teaching syntax.

And I'd add that coding is not just one application among many. If a model can really operate a computer through code, write its own tools, and debug its own mistakes, that's very close to a general capability for acting in the digital world. So I see coding models as kind of the front line for agents overall. Whoever gets coding agents to be truly reliable over long tasks will learn a lot about how to build general intelligence, not just better programmers.

r002.rationale: It says agents should handle work over hours or days, maintain intent across many steps, and iterate, clearly connecting longer work to more demanding development tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the next big step is moving from writing code to actually finishing engineering work. Right now most coding models are very good at the local task: you give them a function, a file, a clear spec, and they produce something reasonable. But real software work is mostly not that. It's understanding a large codebase you didn't write, figuring out which of fifty places a change actually touches, running the tests, reading the failure, going back, and repeating that loop until the thing works end to end. The model has to hold a long horizon of intent and keep correcting itself over hours, not seconds.

So the direction I care about is long-horizon agentic capability, and I'd break it into a few pieces.

First is the training signal. Supervised data from GitHub gets you fluency, but it doesn't teach you to verify. What really moves things is reinforcement learning in environments where the model has to run its code, see real feedback, and get rewarded for the outcome rather than for text that looks right. Verifiable rewards are what make coding such a good domain for this. The compiler and the test suite are honest judges, and we should use them much more aggressively during training.

Second is context and memory. Codebases are millions of lines, and the relevant information is scattered. Pure context window growth helps, but what you really want is the model learning how to navigate: search, read selectively, build a working model of the repository, and remember what it learned earlier in the session. That's a skill, and it can be trained.

Third is efficiency. If the model is going to work for hours on a task, every token matters. Mixture-of-experts, better attention mechanisms, cheaper inference, all of that is not just a cost issue. It determines whether long agentic loops are economically viable at all. A model that's slightly weaker but ten times cheaper can afford to try ten times, verify, and pick the one that works, and that often beats the stronger model that only gets one shot.

And then there's the part people underestimate, which is taste. Good engineers don't just make code pass tests. They make choices about structure, naming, what not to build. Capturing that is harder because there's no clean reward, but I think as models do more end-to-end work, we'll be forced to deal with it, through human feedback, through models judging each other, through learning from how maintainers actually review code.

If I had to compress it: the last few years were about making models good at writing code. The next few are about making them good at being engineers, and that's a very different training problem.

r001.rationale: The response names completing engineering work end to end as the next direction, including navigating a codebase, testing, and iterating until the change works.

r002.rationale: It says models need to sustain intent and self-correction over hours, enabling work beyond short, local coding tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not state that a development task can be complex despite involving little code.

astra-6.text:
I think the next major direction is moving from generating code to completing an entire engineering task. Writing a function is only one part of that. The model needs to understand an existing codebase, clarify what the user wants, make changes across files, and then test whether those changes actually solve the problem.

The key challenge is reliability over longer tasks. If a model makes a mistake early on, can it discover that through testing, understand the cause, and revise its approach? That feedback loop is very important.

So I would pay attention to how well models work with tools and environments, and how we train them to learn from execution results. The goal is for a developer to delegate a meaningful piece of work and receive something they can inspect, verify, and build on.

r001.rationale: It identifies moving from code generation to completing an entire engineering task, including understanding a codebase, changing files, and testing the result.

r002.rationale: It describes completing longer engineering tasks and emphasizes reliability as models work through them, discover mistakes, and revise their approach.

r003.rationale: It does not state that a development task can be complex while involving little code.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next major direction is moving from generating code to completing software engineering tasks. Writing a function is only one part of that. A model needs to understand an existing codebase, clarify the requirements, make changes across files, run tests, and use the results to correct its own mistakes.

The key challenge is reliability over longer tasks. A model can produce a convincing answer in one turn, but can it keep working toward the right goal when its first approach fails? I think progress will depend on models learning to interact with tools and get feedback from real execution, with humans still guiding the important decisions.

r001.rationale: It identifies completing software engineering tasks as the direction and describes an end-to-end workflow across an existing codebase, including changes, tests, and corrections.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability on longer tasks, but does not state that sustained work lets models tackle more complex development tasks.
